title: Art Theory
subtitle: Elements, colour, composition, perspective, light and a tour of movements, with Python labs and two interactive tools
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: A beginner-friendly course in art theory: the elements of art and principles of design, colour basics and harmonies, composition with the rule of thirds and the golden ratio, perspective and depth, light and shadow, and a quick tour of art movements from the Renaissance to the present. Python labs turn colour, composition and perspective into numbers, and two interactive tools let you pick colour harmonies and try composition grids.

chapters.title: Learning to see: what art theory is for
summary: Art theory gives names to what you see and a way to talk about why a picture works. It does not tell you what to make, but it gives you tools to choose with.
Most theory splits into elements, the building blocks (line, shape, form, space, value, texture, colour), and principles, the ways to arrange them (balance, contrast, emphasis, rhythm, unity).
The best way to learn is to look closely, name what you see, and try small studies.

glossary.def: A basic ingredient of an image, such as line, shape, form, space, value, texture or colour.
A way of organising elements, such as balance, contrast, emphasis, movement, rhythm and unity.
The arrangement of elements within the picture.
A structured look at a work: describe, analyse, interpret, judge.
A small practice drawing or painting made to learn one thing.

keyPoints: Elements are the ingredients; principles are the recipe.

items: ELI5. Art has ingredients, like a recipe: lines, shapes, colours, light and dark. The fun part is how you mix them.

When you look at a painting you like, you may only feel that it works. Theory lets you say why. Is it the strong diagonal, the single red coat in a grey crowd, or the way the dark corner holds your eye? Naming these helps you do them yourself.

Artists have used the same toolbox for centuries. The elements are what is on the canvas: lines, shapes, forms, spaces, values, textures and colours. The principles are what the artist does with them: balance, contrast, emphasis, movement, rhythm, pattern and unity.

A good habit is the four-step critique. Describe what you see without judging. Analyse how the elements are used. Interpret what the work seems to mean or feel like. Then judge it, with reasons. Most people start with the last step, but the first one is where learning happens.

Rules like the rule of thirds are guides that work most of the time. Great artists break them on purpose, and the result works because they knew what they broke. Learn the rule, try it, then see what happens when you do the opposite.

This course mixes ideas with small calculations. Python labs turn colour and composition into numbers, so you can see how a warm tone is built or where the golden section falls. Two interactive tools let you pick colour harmonies and try composition grids on your own canvas.

chapters.title: The elements of art
summary: Line is a mark between two points; it can be straight, curved, thick, thin, actual or implied. Shape is a flat area enclosed by a line or a colour change. Form is a shape with depth.
Space is the area around and inside things, both positive (the subject) and negative (the empty area). Value is how light or dark something is. Texture is the feel of a surface, real or drawn.
Colour is the seventh element and has its own chapters. Each element can be used in a drawing to build mood and meaning.

glossary.def: A mark that connects points; it can show edge, movement or direction.
A flat, enclosed area, geometric or organic.
A three-dimensional shape with height, width and depth.
The empty area around and between subjects.
The lightness or darkness of a colour or tone.

keyPoints: Line: straight, curved, thick, thin, implied.
Value: white to black in steps.
Texture can be real or implied.

items: ELI5. A line is the track of a moving dot. A shape is a line that comes home again. Give a shape some thickness and it turns into a thing you could hold.

Draw a line with a pencil and you have already made choices. A straight line feels calm, a zigzag nervous, a curve gentle. A thick line is bold and a thin one delicate. Lines can lead the eye across the page, or hint at a shape that is not drawn, called an implied line.

Close a line into a loop and you get a shape. Geometric shapes like circles and squares feel man-made and orderly. Organic shapes like leaves and clouds feel natural and free. Shading a shape so it seems to have thickness turns it into a form, like a sphere from a circle.

Space includes the room around objects. The subject takes the positive space and the leftover is the negative space. Look at the shape of the empty space between a chair's legs, and it is easier to draw the chair right. Overlap, size and position create the feeling of depth.

Value is the range from light to dark. A drawing in only pencil can look fully 3D just from value. Squint at a picture, and the details melt into a few big value shapes. If the value structure works, the picture works, whatever the colour.

Texture is how a surface feels or seems to feel: rough, smooth, soft, hard. Real texture is thick paint or paper grain. Implied texture is drawn marks that make you imagine touching fur or stone. Contrasting textures next to each other, like silk and rock, make a picture feel alive.

quiz.q: What is the difference between shape and form?

options: How light or dark something is
A line the eye connects without drawing it

quiz.q: What does a squint test show?

practice.title: Value steps
practice.intro: Write value_scale(n): a list of n evenly spaced grey values from 0 (black) to 255 (white), n at least 2. Each value is round(255 x i / (n - 1)) for i from 0 to n - 1.
practice.hint: Divide 255 into n minus 1 equal steps.

practice.title: Negative space ratio
practice.intro: Write negative_ratio(canvas_w, canvas_h, shapes): shapes is a list of [w, h] rectangles that do not overlap. Return the fraction of the canvas not covered, rounded to 3 decimals.
practice.hint: Subtract the used area from the canvas area.

chapters.title: Colour basics
summary: Every colour has three properties: hue (which colour it is), saturation (how vivid) and value (how light). Changing one gives a tint, shade or tone of the same hue.

The traditional primaries are red, yellow and blue. Mixing two gives a secondary (orange, green, violet), and mixing a primary with a neighbouring secondary gives a tertiary. Screens use red, green and blue light; printers use cyan, magenta, yellow and black ink.
Warm colours (reds, oranges, yellows) seem to come forward, and cool colours (blues, greens) seem to recede.

glossary.def: The pure colour name, such as red or blue.
How vivid or grey a colour is.
A hue mixed with white, black or grey.
Colours that cannot be mixed from others; traditionally red, yellow, blue.
Colours opposite each other on the wheel.

keyPoints: Tint = + white. Shade = + black. Tone = + grey.
Opposites on the wheel are complementary.

items: ELI5. Every colour has a name, a brightness and a strength. Add white to be lighter, black to be darker, and grey to be quieter.

Take a tube of red paint. Its hue is red. Add white and it gets lighter, a tint, like pink. Add black and it gets darker, a shade, like maroon. Add grey and it gets duller, a tone. The hue never changed, only its value or saturation.

Painters learn three primaries, red, yellow and blue, that mix to give the other hues. Red and yellow give orange. Yellow and blue give green. Blue and red give violet. Put these on a circle and you have a colour wheel with twelve steps.

The wheel has a warm half and a cool half. Warm colours feel like sun and fire, and they seem to step toward the viewer. Cool colours feel like water and shade, and they seem to step back. Painters use this to build depth: warm in front, cool in the distance.

Screens work differently. They mix light, not paint. Red, green and blue light added together make white. Each colour is written as three numbers from 0 to 255, such as 255, 0, 0 for pure red. A web colour like FF8800 is the same three numbers in hexadecimal.

Printers subtract light instead. Cyan, magenta and yellow inks soak up parts of white light, and black ink adds depth. This is CMYK. Colours that look fine on screen can look duller in print, because ink cannot reach every colour that light can.

quiz.q: What does adding white to a hue make?
Which colours seem to come forward?

quiz.explain: Red and green, blue and orange.

chapters.title: Colour harmony and palettes
summary: Colour harmonies are ways of picking colours that sit well together, found by distances on the colour wheel. Complementary uses opposites, analogous uses neighbours, triadic uses three evenly spaced, and split-complementary uses one hue and the two next to its opposite.
A palette is a limited set of colours for one work. Limiting the palette gives unity.
Contrast matters too: colours with similar values read poorly together, even if the hues contrast.

glossary.def: Two hues opposite each other on the colour wheel.
Hues that sit next to each other on the wheel.
Three hues evenly spaced around the wheel, 120 degrees apart.
The set of colours chosen for a work.
A number comparing the lightness of two colours; higher means easier to read.

keyPoints: Value contrast matters more than hue contrast for legibility.

items: ELI5. Colours sit on a wheel like friends at a table. Some neighbours are calm together, and opposites make each other pop.

Imagine the colour wheel as a clock face with 360 degrees. Red is at 0, yellow near 60, green at 120, cyan at 180, blue at 240 and magenta at 300. Any harmony is just a pattern of angles on this wheel.
Complementary colours are 180 degrees apart, like red and cyan or blue and orange. Side by side they make each other look brighter, which is great for accents. Mixed together they cancel to grey.
Analogous colours are neighbours, within about 30 degrees, and they make a calm, unified look, like a sunset of reds, oranges and yellows.

Triadic harmony picks three colours 120 degrees apart, like red, green and blue. It is lively and balanced, often used in children's art. Split-complementary takes a hue and the two colours on either side of its complement. It has contrast, but is less harsh than a pure complement.

A palette works best when it is limited. A common recipe is 60-30-10: sixty percent a dominant colour, thirty percent a secondary and ten percent an accent. The accent is the pop. Many posters, rooms and websites follow this pattern without saying so.

Do not forget value. Two bright colours of the same value, like red and green at the same lightness, seem to vibrate and are hard to read together. Convert a picture to grey to test it. If shapes vanish, the values are too close.
Design tools measure it with a contrast ratio, and good body text needs a ratio of at least 4.5 to 1.

practice.title: Harmony hues
practice.intro: Write harmony(hue, kind): hue is in degrees 0 to 359. Return the list of hues (each 0 to 359, base first): 'complementary' is [h, h + 180], 'analogous' is [h - 30, h, h + 30], 'triadic' is [h, h + 120, h + 240], 'split' is [h, h + 150, h + 210]. Take every value modulo 360.

practice.title: Contrast ratio
practice.intro: Write contrast(a, b) for two colours as [r, g, b] lists of 0 to 255. Convert each channel c to c/255; if it is at most 0.03928 divide by 12.92, otherwise compute ((c + 0.055) / 1.055) ** 2.4. Luminance L = 0.2126 R + 0.7152 G + 0.0722 B. The ratio is (Lhigh + 0.05) / (Llow + 0.05). Return it rounded to 2 decimals.
practice.hint: Compute the luminance of each colour, then divide.

chapters.title: Principles of design
summary: The principles of design are ways of organising the elements. Balance spreads visual weight. Contrast sets differences against each other. Emphasis creates a focal point. Movement leads the eye. Rhythm and pattern repeat things. Proportion relates sizes. Unity makes it all feel like one piece.
Balance can be symmetrical (mirror-like), asymmetrical (different things of equal weight) or radial (around a centre).
Good design balances unity with variety: enough sameness to feel whole, enough difference to stay interesting.

glossary.def: An even distribution of visual weight across the picture.
The place that grabs attention first.
A visual beat made by repeating elements.
The size relationship between parts and the whole.
The tension between sameness that holds a work together and differences that keep it interesting.

keyPoints: Movement follows lines, edges and gaze.

items: ELI5. A picture is like a seesaw: big light things and small heavy things can balance. One thing should be the star.

Picture a seesaw. A big weight near the middle balances a small weight far out. Pictures work like this. A large pale shape can balance a small dark one, because the dark one pulls harder. Symmetrical balance mirrors both sides, and asymmetrical balance uses different elements of equal pull.

Contrast is difference: light against dark, big against small, smooth against rough, warm against cool. High contrast draws attention, and low contrast calms. A single bright patch in a muted scene becomes the focal point without anything else being said.

Emphasis decides what you see first. Artists make a focal point by contrast, isolation or size. Everything else supports it. If everything shouts, nothing is heard. In a portrait, the face often has the sharpest detail and strongest value contrast.

Movement is how the eye travels. Lines, edges, a pointing arm or a gaze lead the viewer through the picture. Rhythm repeats elements to create a beat: regular like fence posts, flowing like waves, progressive like shapes growing larger. Pattern is rhythm laid across a surface.

Proportion relates sizes, such as head to body, or a figure to its landscape. Unity ties it together by repeating colour, shape or style. Variety keeps it from being dull. The best work has both: a limited palette and a few changes of scale.
Test any picture by asking: what leads, what supports, and what could go.

options: The place that grabs attention first

quiz.q: What does unity need alongside it?

cards.a: the work feels like one piece

practice.title: Visual balance
practice.intro: Write balance(items): items is a list of [weight, x] pairs where x is the distance from the centre of the picture (negative left, positive right). Return the net torque, the sum of weight x x, as a number. Zero means balanced.
practice.hint: Multiply each weight by its distance and add.

practice.title: Rhythm
practice.intro: Write rhythm(sizes): sizes is a list of element sizes in a row. Return 'regular' if all are equal, 'progressive' if they strictly increase or strictly decrease, otherwise 'varied'. A list with one item is 'regular'.
practice.hint: Track whether the list is all equal, always rising or always falling.

chapters.title: Composition: arranging the picture

maps.title: Composition
links: Rule of thirds | places | Subjects on lines
Negative space | gives | Room to breathe
Format | sets | Shape of the canvas

summary: Composition is how you place things inside the frame. A simple guide is the rule of thirds: divide the frame into a three by three grid, and place the subject on a line or where two lines meet.

The golden ratio, about 1.618, is another old guide. Dividing a length in golden proportion puts the dividing point about 0.618 of the way along. Leading lines, framing and negative space help guide the eye.
None of these are laws. They give a starting point and a reason, and good work often bends them.

glossary.def: A guide that divides the frame into thirds in each direction, with the strongest points at the four intersections.
The proportion of about 1.618 to 1, also written phi.
A line in the picture that leads the eye toward the focal point.
The shape and orientation of the canvas, such as portrait, landscape or square.
Using elements inside the picture to surround the subject.

keyPoints: Thirds: lines at 1/3 and 2/3 across and down.
Leading lines lead to the focal point.
Give a moving subject space to move into.

items: ELI5. Put the main thing a bit to the side, not dead centre, and the picture feels alive, like a ball in mid-bounce.

Place a dot in the exact centre of a rectangle. It is stable, but also static and a little dull. Move it to one of the points one third across and one third down, and the picture wakes up. This is the rule of thirds, and cameras still show it as a grid.

To use the grid, put the horizon on the upper or lower line and not in the middle. Put the main subject on an intersection. In a portrait, the eyes often sit on the upper line. Give a person looking left a little more room on the left, called lead room, so the glance has somewhere to go.

The golden ratio comes from dividing a line so that the whole is to the longer part as the longer part is to the shorter. The number is about 1.618. The longer part is then 0.618 of the whole. Many artists use it as a slightly less rigid cousin of thirds.
You can find it in spirals and in the Fibonacci numbers.

Lines carry the eye. A road, river, fence or row of trees can lead from the edge of the frame to the subject. Diagonals feel energetic and horizontals feel calm, while verticals feel strong. A frame within the frame, like an arch or window, adds depth and focus.

The shape of the canvas matters too. Landscape format suits wide scenes and calm. Portrait suits a standing figure and height. A square is neutral and centred. Crop a photo to different shapes and you will see how the mood changes, which is a quick way to practise.

quiz.q: What does the rule of thirds divide?
options: The frame into a 3 x 3 grid

quiz.q: About what is the golden ratio?

options: Guide the eye to the subject
Space in front of a moving or looking subject

practice.title: Composition grid
practice.intro: Tap or drag on the canvas to place the subject. Switch between thirds and golden grids, and place the subject on 3 different strong points to complete this lab.
practice.html: Tap to place the subject.

practice.title: Match the guide
practice.intro: Pair each composition guide with its idea.

practice.title: Thirds points
practice.intro: Write thirds_points(w, h): the four strong intersection points of the rule-of-thirds grid for a w by h canvas. Return them as [[x, y], ...] in the order top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right, with x = w/3 or 2w/3 and y = h/3 or 2h/3, each rounded to 1 decimal.
practice.hint: Compute thirds along each side, then combine.
practice.solution:
def thirds_points(w, h):
    xs = [round(w / 3.0, 1), round(2 * w / 3.0, 1)]
    ys = [round(h / 3.0, 1), round(2 * h / 3.0, 1)]
    return [[xs[0], ys[0]], [xs[1], ys[0]], [xs[0], ys[1]], [xs[1], ys[1]]]

practice.title: Golden section
practice.intro: Write golden_split(length): the point that divides the length in the golden ratio, measured from the start: length x 0.6180339887, rounded to 2 decimals. Also return the other piece. Give [longer, shorter] as a list, with longer = round(length x 0.6180339887, 2) and shorter = round(length - longer, 2).
practice.hint: The longer piece is 0.618 of the whole.
practice.solution:
def golden_split(length):
    longer = round(length * 0.6180339887, 2)
    shorter = round(length - longer, 2)
    return [longer, shorter]

practice.title: Which strong point?
practice.intro: Write nearest_third(w, h, x, y): the index (0 to 3, in the same order top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right) of the thirds intersection nearest to the point (x, y). Break ties by the lower index.
practice.hint: Compare squared distances to all four points.

chapters.title: Perspective and space
summary: Perspective is the art of showing three-dimensional space on a flat surface. The horizon line is your eye level. Parallel lines that go away from you seem to meet at a vanishing point on the horizon.
One-point perspective has a single vanishing point, as when looking straight down a road. Two-point perspective shows a building corner, with two vanishing points.
Without lines, depth also comes from overlap, size, position and atmospheric perspective, where far things become lighter, bluer and less sharp.

glossary.def: The line at the viewer's eye level where sky and ground appear to meet.
A point on the horizon where parallel lines going away appear to meet.
A system with one vanishing point, used for views straight on.
Distant objects look paler, bluer and softer because of the air.
The shortening of forms that point toward the viewer.

keyPoints: Parallel lines meet at a vanishing point.
Far objects: smaller, higher, lighter, bluer.
Overlap shows what is in front.

items: ELI5. Train tracks look like they meet far away. That meeting point sits at the height of your eyes. Far things look small, pale and blue.

Stand on a straight railway track and look down it. The rails seem to come closer together and meet at a point far away. That point is the vanishing point, and it sits on the horizon, at the height of your eyes. If you crouch, the horizon drops with you.

In one-point perspective, a box seen from the front has one face flat to you and its side edges run to a single vanishing point. It suits corridors, roads and rooms. Vertical lines stay vertical and horizontal ones stay horizontal, except those going back in depth.

In two-point perspective, you look at a corner of a box. The vertical edge nearest you is tallest. The top and bottom edges on each side run to separate vanishing points on the horizon. This is the usual setting for buildings.
Three-point perspective adds a third point above or below, for looking up at a tower.

Size shrinks with distance. An object twice as far away appears half the size. You can calculate it: project a point at depth z onto a picture plane at distance d by multiplying its x and y by d divided by z. This is how computer graphics draw 3D worlds.

Even without lines, painters hint at depth. Overlap shows what is in front. Objects higher on the page seem farther away when they stand on the ground. Atmospheric perspective makes far hills pale, blue and soft. Warm, sharp, dark details come forward.
Combining these cues feels more natural than lines alone.

options: At the top of the sky

options: Distant things look paler and bluer

quiz.q: An object twice as far looks...

practice.title: Match the depth cue
practice.intro: Pair each cue with what it does.

practice.title: Project a point
practice.intro: Write project(x, y, z, d): the perspective projection of a 3D point (x, y, z) onto a picture plane at distance d from the eye, with z the depth. Return [x x d / z, y x d / z] rounded to 2 decimals. Assume z is greater than 0.
practice.hint: Divide by the depth.
practice.solution:
def project(x, y, z, d):
    return [round(x * d / z, 2), round(y * d / z, 2)]

practice.title: Apparent size
practice.intro: Write apparent_size(size, distance, ref_distance): the apparent size of an object that has the given size when seen at ref_distance, if moved to distance. The size scales as ref_distance divided by distance. Return it rounded to 3 decimals.
practice.hint: Twice as far means half the size.
practice.solution:
def apparent_size(size, distance, ref_distance):
    return round(size * ref_distance / float(distance), 3)

practice.title: Fade with distance
practice.intro: Write haze(colour, sky, distance, max_distance): mix a colour [r, g, b] toward the sky colour as distance grows. t = min(distance / max_distance, 1). Return [round(c + (s - c) x t)] for each channel as ints.
practice.hint: Reuse the mixing idea with a limit at 1.

chapters.title: Light, shadow and value

maps.title: Light and value
links: Core shadow | is | Darkest on the form
Cast shadow | falls | On other surfaces
Reflected light | softens | The shadow side

summary: Light is what lets us see form. On a rounded object lit from one side, the surface goes from highlight through light and halftone to a core shadow, then a touch of reflected light at the edge, and finally a cast shadow on the ground.
A value scale of five to nine steps from white to black helps judge values. Most strong drawings simplify the many values they see into three or four main groups.
Chiaroscuro, light and dark contrast, was used by painters such as Caravaggio and Rembrandt to give drama and depth.

glossary.def: The brightest spot where light reflects most strongly.
The darkest band on the form, away from the light source.
The shadow an object throws onto another surface.
A faint light bounced back into the shadow side from nearby surfaces.
A strong use of light and dark to model form and create drama.

keyPoints: Order on a sphere: highlight, light, halftone, core shadow, reflected light.
Cast shadow is darkest near the object.
Squint to see the big pattern.

items: ELI5. Light makes a ball look round: bright on one side, dark on the other, and a little glow bouncing back in the dark.

Put an egg on a table and shine a lamp from the upper left. You will see a bright highlight, a broad light area, a gradual halftone, and then a darker band on the side away from the lamp. That darkest band is the core shadow, and it is not at the very edge.

Right at the edge, a bit of light bounces back from the table. This reflected light is weaker than the main light, so it never gets as bright as the lit side. Ignoring it makes forms look flat and cut out. Add it and the form turns round.

The egg also throws a cast shadow on the table. It is darkest and sharpest next to the egg, and softer farther away. The shape of the cast shadow tells you the direction of the light and the shape of the ground it falls on.

To judge values, use a value scale of squares from white to black. Hold a pencil up to compare. Beginners tend to use too few dark values, so everything looks pale. A good plan is to separate the picture into light, middle and dark groups, and give each its own sweep.

Rembrandt and Caravaggio pushed this to the extreme, with figures emerging from deep darkness into a pool of light. The technique is called chiaroscuro, Italian for light-dark. You can use it with a single lamp and a dark background for striking still lifes.

options: On the form, away from the light

practice.intro: Pair each zone with its description.

practice.title: Lambert shading
practice.intro: Write shade(nx, ny, lx, ly, ambient): the brightness of a surface point on a circle. (nx, ny) is the unit surface normal and (lx, ly) the unit direction toward the light. brightness = max(0, nx x lx + ny x ly), then add ambient and return min(1, brightness + ambient), rounded to 3 decimals.

practice.title: Quantise values
practice.intro: Write posterize(values, levels): reduce a list of values 0 to 255 to the given number of levels, 2 or more. Each value maps to round(v / 255 x (levels - 1)) and then back to the grey round(index x 255 / (levels - 1)). Return the list of ints.
practice.hint: Pick the nearest of the evenly spaced greys.

chapters.title: Art movements: a quick tour
summary: Art movements are groups of artists who shared ideas in a time and place. Knowing the main ones shows how the elements and principles have been used differently.

The Renaissance perfected perspective and anatomy. The Baroque added drama with light. Impressionism painted fleeting light and colour. Cubism showed objects from many viewpoints, and abstract art dropped the subject altogether.
A timeline is a map. Place each artist or movement on it, and you start to see how one idea led to the next.

glossary.def: A period from the 14th to 16th century that revived classical ideas and developed linear perspective.
A 17th-century style of drama, movement and strong light and dark.
A 19th-century movement that painted light and colour with quick visible brushstrokes.
An early 20th-century movement that showed subjects from several viewpoints at once.
Art that does not try to show the visible world.

keyPoints: Abstract: form and colour for their own sake.

items: ELI5. Artists in different times cared about different things: real depth, drama, quick light, many viewpoints. Each one answered the last.

In fifteenth-century Italy artists rediscovered the classical world and developed the geometry of perspective. Figures got real weight, and rooms got real depth. Leonardo, Raphael and Michelangelo are the names most people know. The goal was to show the world as it looks, and as it ideally could be.

The Baroque that followed turned up the drama. Figures twist, light cuts through darkness, and everything seems about to move. Caravaggio, Rembrandt and Rubens used chiaroscuro and diagonal compositions to put the viewer in the middle of the action.

In the nineteenth century Impressionists such as Monet and Renoir took their easels outdoors. They painted the changing light, with quick brushstrokes and bright colours placed side by side. A picture became a record of an instant, rather than a polished scene.

In the early twentieth century, Picasso and Braque broke objects into planes seen from several sides, which is Cubism. Others went further. Kandinsky and Mondrian made art from colour, line and shape alone. Surrealists like Dali mixed dream images with precise painting.

Today art uses nearly every medium: photography, video, installation, digital tools. The elements and principles remain. A good way to learn them is to copy a small study from each movement, to feel the choices that artist made, and then make your own.

chapters.title: Critique and a practice routine
summary: Skill grows by looking carefully and making many small studies. A daily routine of ten to twenty minutes beats an occasional long session.
Before a large piece, make several small thumbnail sketches to try different compositions quickly. Use reference, and then change it to make it your own.
Finish by looking at your own work as a critic. Describe, analyse, interpret, judge, and then pick one thing to try next.

glossary.def: A tiny quick sketch used to test a composition.
A small focused exercise on one problem, such as value or colour.
A photo or object you draw from.
A copy of a work by an artist you admire, done to learn their choices.
A book where you practise and record ideas.

keyPoints: Ten minutes a day beats once a month.
Keep dated work to see progress.

items: ELI5. Get better by drawing a little every day, trying small tests, and looking at your own work like a friendly coach.

Most art skills come from seeing better, not from talent. A short daily routine trains the eye. Draw a household object in ten minutes with a pencil. Next day, the same object with only three values. The day after, in a limited palette. Small repeated tries beat rare big ones.

Before you start a big piece, make thumbnails. Draw six small rectangles and sketch the idea in each with a different composition: the subject on the left, on the right, high, low, close, far. Pick the best. This costs five minutes and saves hours.

Study one thing at a time. A value study ignores colour. A colour study ignores detail. A perspective study uses a simple box. Isolating a skill makes it easier to see progress. Combine skills only when each one feels comfortable.

Copy to learn. A master copy of a small part of a painting you admire shows you the choices behind it: why the dark goes there, how the edge is soft. Do it for practice, label it as a study, and then make an original piece that uses what you learned.

Review your work every month. Lay out the pages side by side and use the four-step critique. What improved? What keeps going wrong? Pick one thing to focus on next. Over a year, you will have a record of your progress, and a clearer sense of your own style.
